Given the majority of [[Sigil]]'s population is transitory at any given time, there's a brisk business in being a '''tout''': a guide willing to show visitors around town. They tend to cluster around marketplaces and frequently-used portals.
There's no central licensing authority for touts, so a visitor's taking a risk. Any given tout could be willing to do the job; or they might be getting paid by an innkeeper to direct visitors to a particular tavern or inn; or they might be a plant, ready to lead a visitor into a dark alley where other thieves may be laying in wait.
[[Factotum]]s often serve as touts, albeit beholden to a [[faction]]. Like a tout might be paid separately to direct visitors to particular establishments, factotums will typically direct travelers to locations owned by their faction or its members.
The best touts have a lot of connections, know who to bribe or cajole, and can get their charges into exclusive places, find companionship, arrange visits with prisoners, or gain audiences to see [[factol]]s or other powerful individuals. All, of course, for the right price.
There's a fair amount of overlap between the city's touts and its [[courier]]s; both need to know the city well, and ferry people from one destination to another. One of the better-known touts, {{NPC|Kylie|planar|female|tiefling|thief|8|Free League|n}}<ref name="unc59">{{b|Planescape|Uncaged: Faces of Sigil|pdf=17285|nip=1|page=59}}</ref>, got her start as a courier working for {{NPC|Autochon|planar|male|human|fighter|12|Free League|ne}} the Bellringer<ref name="itc14">{{b|Planescape|In the Cage: A Guide to Sigil|pdf=17274|page=14}}</ref><ref name="unc11">{{b|Planescape|Uncaged: Faces of Sigil|pdf=17285|nip=1|page=11}}</ref><ref name="dvd132">{{b|D&D|Die Vecna Die!|pdf=17483|nip=1|page=132}}</ref> before quitting in the middle of a delivery. Her "crowd" consists of numerous touts, couriers, and [[light boy]]s.

The '''Tower Sorcerous''' is a dark fortress of knowledge and ambition found in [[Sigil]]'s [[Clerk's Ward]], and headquarters to the [[Incanterium]]. A spiny spire whose surface shifts like a puddle of oil, the Tower houses every item and scrap of magical lore which the Wanters could find.
The tower has no visible doors or windows, only eight balconies jutting from its surface. Incantifiers step into and pass through its surface easily.
Other factions would use the Incanterium for help in return for magic. Eventually, there came a time when the factions were dancing to the Incanterium's tune. This seemed to be a breaking point for the [[Lady of Pain]]: one day the Tower Sorcerous was no longer looming over the Ward, leaving behind an empty lot. Some suspected the Lady had tossed the whole Tower and its inhabitants into the [[Maze]]s.
Centuries passed and the Tower was forgotten.
Recently the Tower reappeared, destroying the business that had been erected in its place ([[Fretter's Fetters and Fritters]]), and returning the Incanterium to the landscape of Sigil's factions.

{{Quote|''Sure, I'll give ya the time of day, berk, but it'll cost ya.''|Kor the Merchantile<ref name="APPttO-p26" />}}
==Description== Tradegate was built in the shape of a star and was surrounded by a wall of grey stone. Within the gate-town, old buildings are frequently demolished and new structures built in their place. As a result, the appearance of Tradegate was constantly changing.<ref name="APPttO-p26" />
The center of Tradegate was home to a grand bazaar, a large five-sided plaza with gold and purple tiles laid out like a checkerboard. The bazaar was home to a multitude of booths and stalls and was one of the main trading hubs in the Outlands. Four sides of the plaza were flanked by four large buildings: the Parliament, Tradegate's mint, the armory and barracks and a library. The fifth side of the plaza opened up onto the hotel district, home to the gate-town's many inns.<ref name="APPttO-p26" />
===Gates=== Unique among the gate-towns, the gate found in Tradegate was actually a living creature, a [[bariaur]] who went by the name of Master Trader. He could be found wandering within the forests located near the gate-town. On occasion he ventured to [[Tir na Og]]. If one successfully completed the long, complicated trading process, Master Trader opened the gate to allow passage into Bytopia.<ref name="APPttO-p26" />
==Government== Tradegate was ruled by a council of merchants called the Parliament. They met on a weekly basis and concerned themselves primarily with trading regulations. New members to the council were not elected, rather anyone who was not of an evil [[alignment]], and also had 500,000 [[gold piece]]s, were welcome to join the Parliament.<ref name="APPttO-p26" />
==Trade== Tradegate was aptly named due to the fact it was a major center of commerce. The gate-town minted their own currency, a coin with a star on one side and an engraving of the [[Faerûnian pantheon|Faerûnian god]] [[Ilmater]] on the other. According to the locals, the coin represented the dual nature of Bytopia. Goods were bought and sold via barter or purchase with hard currency, credit was rare and never given to on who was not from the gate-town.<ref name="APPttO-p26" />
==Inhabitants== The inhabitants of Tradegate were primarily [[gnome]]s and [[human]]s, and were an industrious lot with a strong work ethic. Begging and vagrancy were forbidden and punishable by a sentence to a workhouse.<ref name="APPttO-p26" />
==History== At some point, a group of [[adventurer]]s from the [[Prime Material plane|Prime Material]] world of [[Toril]] came to the city of Sigil, having purchased a [[map]] from a sage in [[Shadowdale]]. When the group's [[fighter]] unfolded the map they began scanning it in search of the gate-town Glorium, only to quickly be corrected by his [[rogue]] ally that town headed to [[Gladsheim]] and they were looking for the gate-town to [[Bytopia]]. Watching the adventurers argue among themselves, a peddler emerged from the shadows with a variety of shaped ''[[mimir]]s'' floating about him. He offered a skull-shaped one to the group's fighter, who proceeded to ask it their query and was told what they sought was Tradegate. Impressed, the adventurers paid the peddler for the ''mimir'' and went off on their journey.<ref name="APPttO-p2-3">{{Cite book/A Player's Primer to the Outlands|2-3}}</ref>
==Rumors & Legends== It was rumored across the Outlands that one could purchase [[fiend|fiendish]] equipment and weapons salvaged from the various battlefields of the [[Blood Wars]] at certain stalls in the bazaar. Word was that anyone interested in such purchases had to wear boots with red stripes while within the bazaar. If seen, they were approached and a meeting was scheduled.<ref name="HB">{{Cite book/Hellbound: The Blood War/The Chant of the War|29}}</ref> ==Appendix== ===Appearances=== :;Card Games ::''[[Blood Wars]]'' ===References=== {{Refs}} ===Connections=== {{Outlands}} [[Category:Gate-towns]] [[Category:Towns]] [[Category:Settlements]] [[Category:Locations in the Outlands]]

The '''Transcendent Order''' are a [[faction]] who believe that the mind just gets in the way. Not that it's useless: the mind simply needs to be brought into harmony with the body. Act without thinking, and you act in harmony with the multiverse.
== History ==
Previous factols: * Factol [[Valny Hawkins]]<ref name="fm142">{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|page=142}}</ref><ref name="fm145">{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|page=145}}</ref>
After the [[Faction War]], the remnants of the faction -- who have long championed the resolution of conflict with words and not clubs -- help set up the [[Sigil Advisory Council]], with former factol [[Rhys]] as one of the first officials in the new Council. In order to not give the impression of the former Transcendent Order having undue influence, they argue against hosting meetings of the Council at the Great Gymnasium.<ref name="fw121122">{{b|Planescape|Faction War (book)|alt=Faction War|pdf=17299|page=121-122}}</ref>
== Philosophy ==
Action without thought is the purest response. Train body and mind to act in harmony, and the spirit becomes ones with the multiverse.
== Role ==
== Membership == : ''See also:'' [[List of Transcendent Order members]]
; '''[[Namer]]s'''
The entrance requirement is pretty easy: walking up to an existing Cipher and asking to join. The faction believes that this is enough to prove that someone knows what they want, and the faction is it. Once in, namers are mostly left to their own devices.
''Benefits'': All Ciphers gain a -1 modifier to initiative rolls.
; '''[[Factotum]]s'''
Factotums are known as '''masters of the heart''' (or simply "heart masters"). They must be at least 3rd level with recognition from their peers for actively trying to unify mind and body.
''Benefits'': Heart masters can place themselves in an "action trance" during an initiative phase, during which they act on reflex alone. They gain +1 on saving throws vs mild-altering spells and effects.
; '''[[Factor]]s'''
Factors are '''masters of the mind''', attained by being at least 7th level, and spending three to four months in solitary training.
''Benefits'': Mind masters get a -2 modifier to initiative, and a +2 on saving throws vs mild-altering spells and effects. In addition, they can call up the action trance at will.
; '''[[Factol]]'''
Dubbed the '''masters of the spirit''', When a new factol needs to be chosen, the other two levels simply decide. There's no meetings or arguments. A master of the spirit feels compelled. Never have the masters decided on a candidate who did not the urge, nor have two felt the compulsion at the same time. The faction simply feels the collective instinct to lead them to the same conclusion.
''Benefits'': Spirit masters get a -3 modifier to initiative, and a +3 on saving throws vs mild-altering spells and effects. In addition, they can call up the action trance at will. They automatically enter an action trance the round before an encounter begins.
; '''Current Factol''' * 2nd Edition: {{NPC|Rhys|planar|female|tiefling|fighter|15|class2=mage|level2=15|Transcendent Order|n}}<ref name="pscs-pg29">{{b|Planescape|Planescape Campaign Setting|pdf=176267|nip=1|page=29}}, ''A Player's Guide to the Planes''</ref><ref name="itc14">{{b|Planescape|In the Cage: A Guide to Sigil|pdf=17274|page=14}}</ref><ref name="fm5">{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|nip=1|page=5}}</ref><ref name="fm142-149">{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|nip=1|page=142-149}}</ref><ref name="fw41">{{b|Planescape|Faction War (book)|alt=Faction War|pdf=17299|page=41}}</ref><ref name="fw121">{{b|Planescape|Faction War (book)|alt=Faction War|pdf=17299|page=121}}</ref><ref name="dmgii192">{{b|D&D|Dungeon Master's Guide 2|pdf=144108|page=192}}</ref> * 5th Edition: {{NPC|Rhys||female|tiefling|Transcendent Order contuit||Transcendent Order|n}}<ref name="paitm-sao28">{{b|Planescape|Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse|page=28}}, ''Sigil and the Outlands''</ref><ref name="paitm-sao54">{{b|Planescape|Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse|page=54}}, ''Sigil and the Outlands''</ref>

'''Transitive Planes''' is a collective term used to describe those [[planes of existence]] that connected other planes together, or could be used as a means of travel between points on a single plane.<ref name="DMG3.5-147">{{Cite book/Dungeon Master's Guide v.3.5|147}}</ref> The various [[cosmology]] models each described them differently and ascribed them slightly different [[Planar traits|traits]], but all were accessed by either magic spells, spell-like abilities, or portals.<ref name="MotP3e-45">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|45}}</ref> The known Transitive Planes were: * The [[Astral Plane]], which later became the [[Astral Sea]] * The [[Ethereal Plane]], which was destroyed by the [[Spellplague]] * The [[Plane of Shadow]], which later became the [[Shadowfell]] * The [[Spirit World]], which only connected to [[Kara-Tur]]<ref name="PGtF-165">{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|165}}</ref><ref name="MotP3e-206">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|206}}</ref> * The [[Plane of Mirrors]], which connected to the back of reflective surfaces<ref name="dof-p33-34">{{Cite book/Dragons of Faerûn|33-34}}</ref><ref name="edwp-p208-209">{{Cite book/Expedition to the Demonweb Pits|208-209}}</ref><ref name="pom-p204-205">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|204-205}}</ref>
Each had their own unique structure and means of travel, and each connected a different set of planes together.

The '''Tribe of One''', more frequently called '''Communals''', were a [[faction]] that believed everyone, no matter their species or profession, was equal. And as equals, we should all share. Knowledge, possessions, even power.
== History ==
The Tribe were largely doing fine until the faction's leadership declared that Sigil belonged to everyone. The [[Lady of Pain]] disagreed. One day the Communals all vanished from the City Provisioner's. It's unknown if the Lady sent them to the Mazes, or if they were otherwise "disappeared." Some say that, as a communal faction, the Lady blamed the entire Tribe for the careless words of a single leader.
== Philosophy ==
== Role ==
The Communals controlled the [[City Provisioner's]], the city's only storehouse of food and grains.
== Membership ==
Membership often came from among the city's poor, who had little other representation among city affairs. Hence the nickname "Hivers," because it was widely accepted that the denizens of the [[Hive Ward]] were likely Communals.
== Background Information ==
* Since the faction appealed to the city's poor, who wanted better representation in the city's politics, it's likely that the faction existed post-[[Great Upheaval]], after factions took over the running of the city from the [[guild]]s. * In ''[[Dark Sun]]'', a "tribe of one" is how Athasians refer to someone with DID: dissociative identity disorder (formerly MPD: multiple personality disorder). It's also the title of a [[w:c:darksun:Tribe of One|novel trilogy by Simon Hawke]], whose protagonist Sorak is a tribe of one.

==Description== Tridrones were shaped like inverted tetrahedrons and were capable of performing three tasks at a time.<ref name="MM5e-p224" />
==Personality== Like all modrons, tridrones had an absolute sense of hierarchy and order, and could not be persuaded to disobey their instructions or betray their purpose in any way.<ref name="MM5e-p224" />
It was possible, however, for a defective tridrone to go rogue and start acting in its own interests or no longer in accordance with its instructions, sometimes even becoming violent. Such rogues were relentlessly hunted by other modrons, although, unlike their properly operating fellows, they could be reasoned with.<ref name="MM5e-p224" />
==Biology== In addition to their [[True seeing|truesight]],<ref name="MM5e-p224" /> tridrones were capable of seeing the [[Infravision|infrared]] and [[Ultravision|ultraviolet spectrums]] out to {{SI|90|ft|long=yes}} and {{SI|100|yards|long=yes}}, respectively.<ref name="MM21e-p88" />
==Abilities== Like all modrons, tridrones were immune to all effects and spells that influenced the mind, fear and attacks that rely on energy from either the [[Negative Energy plane|Negative]] or [[Positive Energy plane|Positive]] energy planes. They also had a resistance to acid, cold and [[fire]].<ref name="TGMM">{{Cite book/The Great Modron March|126}}</ref>
==Combat== Tridrones were capable of wielding weapons and were competent combatants, capable of performing three attacks at a time. If destroyed, a tridrone disintegrated completely into dust and a [[duodrone]] was instantly upgraded into a tridrone to fill its position.<ref name="MM5e-p224" /> One of the weapons most commonly wielded by them were [[javelin]]s, which they would hurl at their foes before closing.<ref name="MM21e-p88" />
==History== Sometime in the late 1480s [[DR]], a tridrone leading a group of [[monodrone]]s was stranded in the [[Labyrinth]] in the [[Underdark]], separated from the other modrons since the previous [[Great Modron March]], over two centuries earlier. After years of wandering, the tridrone managed to keep the group together, but felt responsible for its failure in performing their assigned task.<ref name="OotA5e-p179-180,183-184" />
==Society== Tridrones could communicate with other tridrones and with [[duodrone]]s and [[quadrone]]s. They were incapable of communicating directly with [[monodrone]]s and could not comprehend the more advanced [[pentadrone]]s.<ref name="MM5e-p224" />
In modron society, tridrones were responsible for leading groups of lesser modrons into battle. They were always created as the result of upgraded duodrones to take the place of destroyed units.<ref name="MM5e-p224" />
There were about six million tridrones in modron society.<ref name="MM21e-p86">{{Cite book/Monster Manual II (1983)|86}}</ref>

This small round stone is the "Unbroken Circle of Zerthimon." The Unbroken Circle is a *zerth* religious text, containing teachings of Zerthimon, the founder of the githzerai people. The Circle is made up of a series of interlocking circles that fold out from one another, depending on which branch the reader wishes to follow in the path of teachings... it is said that some *zerths* spend years poring over the combinations of the plates, looking for new significance in the teachings. Dak'kon seems to use the text as a means of focusing his spell casting abilities, for he pores over the tablet occasionally, memorizing the words.
The '''Unbroken Circle of Zerthimon''' is a [[zerth]] religious text in the form of a series of interlocking circular stone plates. Puzzling out how they fold, spin, and interlock, allows the reader to discover new writings, collectively the [[Way of Zerthimon]]. It is said that some zerths spend years poring over the combinations of the plates, looking for new significance in the teachings. A reader may additionally pull out individual unlocked discs in order to learn the lessons as wizard spells. Curiously, removing plates in this manner does not appear to affect the size of the circle, and in fact multiple copies can be withdrawn to no apparent change.
[[Dak'kon]]'s copy of the Unbroken Circle was gifted to him by the Practical Incarnation of [[The Nameless One]], with whom Dak'kon travelled in the past.
If the Nameless One is a magic-user, he may speak to Dak'kon about learning the Way of Zerthimon via the Unbroken Circle.
== The Lessons == Each circle is successively more challenging to unlock, such that a reader will unlock each lesson in order.
=== The First Circle ===
: Know ''that we are the [[First People]]. Once all was chaos. The First People were thought drawn from chaos. When the First People came to ''know'' themselves, they were chaos no longer, and became flesh. With their thoughts and ''knowing'' of matter, the People shaped the [[First World]] and dwelled there with their ''knowing'' to sustain them.''
: ''Yet the flesh was new to the People and with it, the People came not to ''know'' themselves. The flesh gave rise to new thoughts. Greed and hates, pains and joys, jealousies and doubts. All of these fed on each other and the minds of the People were divided. In their division, the People were punished.''
: ''The emotions of the flesh were strong. The greed and hates, the pains and joys, the jealousies and doubts, all of these served as a guiding stone to enemies. In becoming flesh, the First People became enslaved to those who ''knew'' flesh only as tools for their will. ''Know'' these beasts were the ''[[illithid]]s''.''
: ''The ''illithids'' were a race that had come not to ''know'' themselves. They had learned how to make other races not ''know'' themselves. They were the tentacled ones. They lived in flesh and saw flesh as tools for their will. Their blood was as water and they shaped minds with their thoughts. When the ''illithids'' came upon the People, the People were a people no more. The People became slaves.''
: ''The ''illithids'' took the People from the First World and brought them to the [[Prime Material plane|False Worlds]]. As the People labored upon the False Worlds, the ''illithids'' taught them the [[Way of the Flesh]]. Through them, the People came to ''know'' loss. They came to ''know'' suffering. They came to ''know'' death, both of the body and mind. They came to ''know'' what it is to be the herd of another and have their flesh consumed. They came to ''know'' the horror of being made to feel joy in such things.''
: ''The Unbroken Circle is the ''knowing'' of how the People lost themselves. And how they came to ''know'' themselves again.''
* '''Lesson''': Strength lies in ''knowing'' oneself. Once someone does not ''know'' themselves, they are lost. They become a tool for others. * '''XP Reward''': 300 XP
=== The Second Circle ===
: Know'' that flesh cannot mark steel. ''Know'' that steel may mark flesh. In ''knowing'' this, [[Zerthimon]] became free.''
: Know'' that the tentacled ones were of flesh. They relied on the flesh and used it as tools for their will. One of the places where flesh served their will was the [[Fields of Husks]] on the [[Prime Material plane|False Worlds]] of the ''[[illithid]]s''.''
: ''The Fields were where the bodies of the [[First People|People]] were cast after the ''illithids'' had consumed their brains. When the brain had been devoured, the husks came to be fertilizer to grow the poison-stemmed grasses of the ''illithids.'' Zerthimon worked the Fields with no ''knowing'' of himself or what he had become. He was a tool of flesh, and the flesh was content.''
: ''It was upon these Fields that Zerthimon came to ''know'' the scripture of steel. During one of the turnings, as Zerthimon tilled the Fields with his hands, he came across a husk whose brain remained within it. It had not been used as food. Yet it was dead. The thought that one of the husks had died a death without serving as food for the ''illithids'' was a thought Zerthimon had difficulty understanding. From that thought, came a desire to ''know'' what had happened to the husk.''
: ''Embedded in the skull of the husk was a steel blade. It had pierced the bone. Zerthimon realized that was what had killed the husk. The steel had marked the flesh, but the flesh had not marked the steel. Zerthimon took the blade and studied its surface. In it, he saw his reflection. It was in the reflection of the steel that Zerthimon first ''knew'' himself. Its edge was sharp, its will the wearer's. It was the blade that would come to be raised against [[Gith]] when Zerthimon made the [[Pronouncement of Two Skies]].''
: ''Zerthimon kept the blade for many turnings, and many were the thoughts he had about it. He used it in the fields to aid his work. In using it, he thought about how it was not used. The ''illithids'' were powerful. Zerthimon had believed that there was nothing that they did not ''know''. Yet the ''illithids'' never carried tools of steel. They only used flesh as tools. Everything was done through flesh, for the tentacled ones were made of flesh and they ''knew'' flesh. Yet steel was superior to flesh. When the blade had killed the husk, it was the flesh that had been weaker than the steel.''
: ''It was then that Zerthimon came to ''know'' that flesh yielded to steel. In ''knowing'' that, he came to ''know'' that steel was stronger than the ''illithids''.''
: ''Steel became the scripture of the People. ''Know'' that steel is the scripture by which the People came to ''know'' freedom.''
* '''Lesson''': (12+ Wis) Not ''knowing'' something can be a tool, just like flesh and steel, if upon encountering it, you attempt to ''know'' its nature and how it came to be. * '''XP Reward''': 600 XP * '''Spell Reward''': The [[Scripture of Steel]]
=== The Third Circle ===
It seems that the first three circles are introductory lessons, of a sort: it's only when you complete the Third Circle that [[Dak'kon]] seems surprised that you're willing to follow the [[Way of Zerthimon]].
: ''[[Zerthimon]] labored many turnings for the ''[[illithid]]'' [[Arlathii Twice-Deceased]] and his partnership in the cavernous heavens of the [[Prime Material plane|False Worlds]]. His duties would have broken the backs of many others, but Zerthimon labored on, suffering torment and exhaustion.''
: ''It came to pass that the ''illithid'' Arlathii Twice-Deceased ordered Zerthimon before him in his many-veined galleria. He claimed that Zerthimon had committed slights of obstinance and cowardice against his partnership. The claim had no weight of truth, for Arlathii only wished to ''know'' if flames raged within Zerthimon's heart. He wished to ''know'' if Zerthimon's heart was one of a slave or of a rebel.''
: ''Zerthimon surrendered to the ''illithid'' punishment rather than reveal his new-found strength. He ''knew'' that were he to show the hatred in his heart, it would serve nothing, and it would harm others that felt as he. He chose to endure the punishment and was placed within the [[Pillars of Silence]] so he might suffer for a turning.''
: ''Lashed upon the Pillars, Zerthimon moved his mind to a place where pain could not reach, leaving his body behind. He lasted a turning, and when he was brought before Arlathii Twice-Deceased, he gave gratitude for his punishment to the ''illithid'' as was custom. In so doing, he proved himself a slave in the ''illithid'' eyes while his heart remained free.''
: ''By enduring and quenching the fires of his hatred, he allowed Arlathii Twice-Deceased to think him weak. When the time of the [[Rising]] came, Arlathii was the first of the ''illithid'' to ''know'' death by Zerthimon's hand and die a third death.''
* '''Lesson''': (14+ Wis) Endure. In enduring, grow strong. * '''XP Reward''': 900 XP * '''Spell Reward''': [[Submerge the Will]]
=== The Fourth Circle ===
: Know'' that the [[Rising]] of the People against the ''[[illithid]]'' was a thing built upon many ten-turnings of labor. Many of the People were gathered and taught in secret the ways of defeating their ''illithid'' masters. They were taught to shield their minds, and use them as weapons. They were taught the scripture of steel, and most importantly, they were given the ''knowing'' of freedom.''
: ''Some of the People learned the nature of freedom and took it into their hearts. The ''knowing'' gave them strength. Others feared freedom and kept silent. But there were those that ''knew'' freedom and ''knew'' slavery, and it was their choice that the People remain chained. One of these was [[Vilquar]].''
: ''Vilquar saw no ''freedom'' in the Rising, but opportunity. He saw that the ''illithid'' had spawned across many of the [[Prime Material plane|False Worlds]]. Their Worlds numbered so many that their vision was turned only outwards, to all they did not already touch. Vilquar's eye saw that much took place that the ''illithid'' did not see. To the Rising, the ''illithid'' were blinded.
: ''Vilquar came before his master, the ''illithid'' [[Zhijitaris]], with the ''knowing'' of the Rising. Vilquar added to his chains and offered to be their eyes against the Rising. In exchange, Vilquar asked that he be rewarded for his service. The ''illithid'' agreed to his contract.
: ''At the bonding of the contract, a dark time occurred. Many were the betrayals Vilquar committed and many were the People that the ''illithids'' fed upon to stem the Rising. It seemed that the Rising would die before it could occur, and the ''illithid'' were pleased with Vilquar's eye.''
: ''It was near the end of this dark time when [[Zerthimon]] came to ''know'' Vilquar's treacheries. In ''knowing'' Vilquar's eye, Zerthimon forced the Rising to silence itself, so that Vilquar might think at last his treacheries had succeeded, and the Rising had fallen. He ''knew'' that Vilquar's eye was filled only with the reward he had been promised. He would see what he wished to see.''
: ''With greed beating in his heart, Vilquar came upon the ''illithid'' Zhijitaris and spoke to his master of his success. He said that the Rising had fallen, and the ''illithids'' were safe to turn their eyes outwards once more. He praised their wisdom in using Vilquar's eye, and he asked them for his reward.''
: ''In his greed-blindness, Vilquar had forgotten the ''knowing'' of why the People had sought freedom. He had lost the ''knowing'' of what slavery meant. He had forgotten what his ''illithid'' masters saw when they looked upon him. And so Vilquar's betrayal of the People was ended with another betrayal. Vilquar came to ''know'' that when Vilquar's eye had nothing left to see, Vilquar's eye was useless.''
: ''The ''illithid'' gave to Vilquar his reward, opening the cavity of his skull and devouring his brain. Vilquar's corpse was cast upon the [[Fields of Husks]] so its blood might water the poison-stemmed grasses.''
* '''Lesson''': (15+ Wis) When one chooses to see only what is before them, they see only a part of the whole. They are blind. And just as Vilquar was blinded by his promised reward, so were the ''illithids'' blinded to the true Rising. For when they heard Vilquar's words, they turned their sight outwards again, and the Rising was free to strike. * '''XP Reward''': 1500 XP * '''Spell Reward''': [[Vilquar's Eye]]
=== The Fifth Circle ===
: ''[[Zerthimon]] was the first to ''know'' the way of freedom. Yet it was not he that first came to ''know'' the way of rebellion.''
: ''The ''knowing'' of rebellion came to the warrior-queen [[Gith]], one of the People. She had served the ''[[illithids]]'' upon many of the [[Prime Material plane|False Worlds]] as a soldier, and she had come to ''know'' war and carried it in her heart. She had come to ''know'' how others might be organized to subjugate others. She ''knew'' the paths of power, and she ''knew'' the art of taking from the conquerors the weapons by which they could be defeated. Her mind was focused, and both her will and her blade were as one.
: ''The turning in which Zerthimon came to ''know'' Gith, Zerthimon ceased to ''know'' himself. Her words were as fires lit in the hearts of all who heard her. In hearing her words, he wished to ''know'' war. He ''knew'' not what afflicted him, but he ''knew'' he wished to join his blade to Gith. He wished to give his hate expression and share his pain with the ''illithid''.''
: ''Gith was one of the People, but her ''knowing'' of herself was greater than any Zerthimon had ever encountered. She ''knew'' the ways of flesh, she ''knew'' the ''illithids'' and in ''knowing'' herself, she was to ''know'' how to defeat them in battle. The strength of her ''knowing'' was so great, that all those that walked her path came to ''know'' themselves.''
: ''Gith was but one. Her strength was such that it caused others to ''know'' their strength. And Zerthimon laid his steel at her feet.''
* '''Lesson''': (16+ Wis) There is great strength in numbers, but there is great power in one, for the strength of the will of one may gather numbers to it. There is strength not only in ''knowing'' the self, but ''knowing'' how to bring it forth in others. * '''XP Reward''': 3000 XP * '''Spell Reward''': The [[Power of One]]
=== The Sixth Circle ===
* '''Lesson''': (18+ Wis) Zerthimon's devotion to the People was such that he was willing to protect them from themselves. He knew the ''illithids'' had come not to ''know'' themselves in their obsession with control and domination. So he chose to stop Gith before she carried the People to their deaths. There must be balance in all things, or else the self will not hold. * '''XP Reward''': 5000 XP * '''Spell Reward''': [[Balance in All Things]]
This Circle causes Dak'kon some strife: he feels as though Zerthimon's will was not submerged, but subverted, by [[Arlathii Twice-Deceased]] (the Third Circle), and the lesson of the virtue of betrayal (the Fourth Circle) was merely laying the groundwork to justify Zerthimon's betrayal of the People, seemingly with the purpose of protecting the illithids from destruction.
He says he once ''knew'' this lesson, but ''knows'' it no longer. In any case, it is the limit of his knowledge. He has not discovered any further Circles.
=== The Seventh Circle ===
This Circle can be discovered by playing with the Unbroken Circle to find undiscovered combinations (16+ Int).
* '''Lesson''': (19+ Wis) Time is an ally, not an enemy. Patience can sharpen even the smallest of efforts into a weapon that can strike the heart of an empire. Your victories may be small, but over time, a greater victory may be achieved. * '''XP Reward''': 8000 XP (3000 XP for discovering the Circle, 5000 XP for learning the lesson) * '''Spell Reward''': [[Missile of Patience]]
=== The Eighth Circle === This Circle can be discovered by playing with the Unbroken Circle to find undiscovered combinations (18+ Int).
* '''Lesson''': (19+ Wis) Focus and discipline are important: Not ''knowing'' oneself can physically divide the man. Weakness causes division: Not only ''know'' yourself and take strength from that, but your focus can reveal weaknesses in your enemy. * '''XP Reward''': 16,000 XP (6000 XP for discovering the Circle, 10,000 XP for learning the lesson, plus 10,000 XP for Dak'kon) * '''Spell Reward''': [[Zerthimon's Focus]] * '''Companion Reward''': Dak'kon gains +1 Strength, +2 Dexterity, +2 Constitution.
Revealing the Eighth Circle to Dak'kon resolves the crisis of faith he developed regarding the Sixth Circle enough that it boosts his stats, and years seem to be shed from his face.
== Background Information == * It's not known if the Unbroken Circle contains additional lessons. Only eight are available in ''Torment''. * The Practical Incarnation refers to the Unbroken Circle as "a collection of lies," and says it was a simple week's work to forge the Circle, implying both that he created it and that it was a forgery, meant only to give Dak'kon sufficient faith to let him use his [[Dak'kon's zerth blade|zerth blade]]. Dak'kon was already a ''zerth'' and would have been familiar with some of [[Zerthimon]]'s teachings, so the teachings in the Circle must have been accurate to some degree in order to fool him. Even the Practical Incarnation admits "perhaps they carry some truth - I know not. I know that they were tedious writings," suggesting that he didn't make up the content, but got them elsewhere. The Circle's inventory description certainly implies that it's a common item among zerths. * The canon history of the githzerai and githyanki has been similar, but none of the portrayals have been totally consistent. After the publication of {{b|Planescape|Planescape: Torment}}, however, the Unbroken Circle's version of events appears to have been accepted as the standard canon, despite the possibility of them being at least partially made up by the Practical Incarnation.

'''Undersigil''' (sometimes styled "UnderSigil"), also known as the '''Realms Below''' isn't formally one of [[Sigil]]'s Wards, but is nonetheless an important region to consider, with a number of its own distinct locations.
Undersigil is the name collectively given to a series of passages, sewers, and catacombs carved or built under the streets of Sigil.
== Location ==
Undersigil was located "in" several other wards, simply beneath the surface of the streets. Each ward had access to it, although it should be noted that not all parts of Undersigil were continuous. One noble family's burial chambers in the Lady's Ward, for example, may not have any connection to any other part of Undersigil, similarly to how a prime world's dungeons, sewer systems, and drow passages aren't all connected to one another.
Some say that the entire torus of Sigil is a dabus warren. The city we see on the surface is just what the city shows to travelers, but the real city is the mass of tunnels, storehouses, dungeons, and corridors beneath the surface. <ref name="itc14">{{b|Planescape|In the Cage: A Guide to Sigil|pdf=17274|page=14}}</ref>

== Background Information == * Sigil has taken two forms over the years: being built on the inner ring of a thick stone "donut," and being built on the inner surface of a tire. The former has ample space for Undersigil; the volume of Undersigil is far greater than the surface area of the city. The latter, however, has only a thin surface on which the city is built; any passages underground (basements, sewers, catacombs, etc) are actually passages to another reality, with new excavations being expensive and rare. In this setup, "Undersigil" is less its own area of the city and more a series of pocket dimensions, similar to the Lady's Mazes.<ref name="dmgii188">{{b|D&D|Dungeon Master's Guide 2|pdf=144108|page=188}}</ref>

The '''upper planes''' (sometimes '''Upper Planes''') was a collective term used in the [[Great Wheel cosmology]] model to represent the [[Outer planes]] of [[Good]] alignment, located across the top of the Great Wheel. These were [[Arcadia]], [[Mount Celestia]], [[Bytopia]], [[Elysium]], the [[Beastlands (plane)|Beastlands]], [[Arborea]], and [[Ysgard]].<ref name="MotP1e-73">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 1st edition|73}}</ref> [[Image:GreatWheel.jpg|thumb|600px|center|The Great Wheel of the Outer Planes]]
The [[World Tree cosmology]] model rearranged, renamed, and reorganized the upper planes into the [[Celestial planes]] but some people still used the older term to describe the good-aligned planes.

The '''Verdant Guild''' are a [[sect]] who believe in the protection and preservation of the wilderness. Without the resources of the wilderness, civilization is doomed, so it must be protected from civilization, evil, and destruction.
== History ==
Founded centuries ago by the centaur ranger [[Angeliika Silverman]].
== Philosophy ==
Wylders seek the preservation of the wilderness, but they're not out to burn down cities; optimally, they want everything to exist in balance with each other, with a healthy respect for the wilderness, and avoiding nature's callous destruction.

The '''Vile Hunt''' are a [[sect]] who can't stand the idea that a simple beast might be smarter than they area. Petitioners in the [[Beastlands (plane)|Beastlands]] -- intelligent minds in animal bodies -- are an abomination, and must be destroyed.
== History ==
The Vile Hunt has only recently appeared, making its presence known in [[Faunel]].
== Philosophy ==
The Vile Hunt are insulted by the very idea of intelligent animals. This makes the Beastlands the prime target of their ire. They make regular hunting parties into the plane, but know better than to stay there for any length of time.

A '''Ward''' is one of five or six geographical distinctions used to slice up the city of [[Sigil]] into distinct districts. They are, proceeding clockwise:
* [[The Lady's Ward]] * The [[Lower Ward]] * The [[Hive Ward]] * The [[Clerk's Ward]] * The [[Guildhall Ward|Guildhall]] and [[Market Ward]]s
A unofficial seventh ward, [[Undersigil]], covers all the catacombs, sewers, tombs, and warrens built beneath the city streets.
The Guildhall and Market Wards are the smallest, and are usually mentioned in the same breath, treated as a single ward. At some point, "Guildhall" gets dropped entirely and the whole area becomes known simply as the Market Ward, with the combined size making it the largest of the five.

When a petitioner was slain in combat during one of the endless chaotic battles, he or she rose again on the team that brought him or her down.<ref name="PGF3e-p163-164" />
The terrain of Warrior's Rest was similar to rocky badlands on the [[Prime Material plane]]. However, the nearby terrain could be manipulated by the will of those with sufficient wisdom to provide cover and other tactical advantages for battle.<ref name="PGF3e-p163-164" />
==Inhabitants== Many [[titan]]s were native to Warrior's Rest, and they joined in the ongoing battle with joy.<ref name="PGF3e-p163-164" /> Also, [[githzerai]] built a fortress and several [[monasteries]] amid the chaotic battles.<ref name="Dr378-p81">{{Cite dragon/378/Playing Githzerai|81}}</ref>
==Petitioners== The petitioners of Warrior's rest included soldiers, generals, strategists, [[barbarian]]s, and many other combat oriented individuals. They appeared as they did in the prime of their lives and in the peak of their physical shape, glowing with health. All sought union with their deity through participation in the great wars, and so were granted extraordinary resilience to [[acid]], [[fire]], cold, and electricity damage, as well as regenerative powers.<ref name="PGF3e-p163-164" />
==Deities== ; [[Beshaba]] : Lady Doom placed [[Blood Tor]], her black [[granite]] tower, atop a high peak overlooking the sea. The blood of accident victims spilled from the mouth of a stag's head statue near the top of the structure. The saints of her faith, the Lysinterai, wreaked endless havok across the plane.<ref name="FRCG4e-p65" /> ; [[Garagos]] : The Reaver declared that whatever region he happened to be currently in is his own realm called [[Battle Garde]].<ref name="PGF3e-p163-164" /> ; [[Red Knight]] : The Lady of Strategy built a fortress called [[Red Tower]] in Warrior's Rest. It was a permanent feature of the plane. The realm and a surrounding radius of 1 mi (1.6 km) could not be manipulated by any creature except by Tempus.<ref name="PGF3e-p163-164" /> ; [[Tempus]] : While the entire plane of Warrior's Rest was considered the realm of The Lord of Battles, he allowed the other deities who resided here to shape the plane how they wished. He could easily undo anything they had done.<ref name="PGF3e-p163-164" /> ; [[Uthgar]] : According to the World Tree Cosmology, The Battle Father resided in the colder regions of Warrior's Rest which he called [[Uthgardtheim]]. This realm was only as cold as a normal winter in the northern regions of Faerûn.<ref name="PGF3e-p163-164" /> ; [[Valkur]] : [[Safe Harbor]], the realm of the Captain of the Waves, was the only realm separate from the others. His was a placid sea of saltwater that separated the rocky battlefield deserts from the a larger expanse of water where the naval battles were waged.<ref name="PGF3e-p163-164" />
==Access to Warrior's Rest== There were no known ''[[portals]]'' to or from Warrior's Rest.<ref name="PGF3e-p163-164" />

[[Winter wolf|Winter wolves]] | languages = | basicrefs = {{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|181}}{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|98}}{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn}} | type-GW = Realm | shape-size-GW = | gravity-GW = | time-GW = | morphic-GW = | element-energy-GW = | alignment-GW = | magical-GW = | layers-GW = | layer-number-GW = | location-GW = [[Pandesmos]] | refs-GW = | type-WA = | shape-size-WA = | gravity-WA = | mutability-WA = | element-energy-WA = | alignment-WA = | magical-WA = | layers-WA = | layer-number-WA = | location-WA = | refs-WA = | type-WT = Realm | shape-size-WT = | gravity-WT = | time-WT = | morphic-WT = Divinely | element-energy-WT = Cold-dominant | alignment-WT = Strongly evil-aligned | magical-WT = | faith-WT = Mild | layers-WT = | layer-number-WT = | location-WT = [[Fury's Heart]] | refs-WT = | inhabitants = | deities = yes | locations = | organizations = | settlements = | usethe = | useon = }} '''Winter's Hall''' was the palace{{Cite dragon/367/Hall of the Frostmaiden|59-61}} and realm of [[Auril]] Goddess of Winter. ==Cosmology== [[File:Yggdrasil Illustration.png|thumb|273px|''An artistic rendition of Yggdrasil, featuring Winter's Hall beneath.'']] In the [[Great Wheel cosmology]], Winter's Hall was found on the layer of [[Pandesmos]] in the plane of [[Pandemonium]].{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Set/Cyclopedia of the Realms|10}} A branch of [[Yggdrasil]], the World Ash, extended to the realm and was said to form the central supporting beam of the hall.{{Cite book/Planes of Chaos/The Book of Chaos|94, 104}} In the [[World Tree cosmology]], her palace was located in [[Fury's Heart]], across from the [[Towers of Ruin]] over the [[Land of the Hunt]]. Between the aftermath of the [[Spellplague]] and the [[Second Sundering]], as part of the [[World Axis cosmology]], Auril's palace was said to hover over the [[Deep Wild]]s, bringing winter with it. The northernmost reaches of the Wilds were known as Tír fo Leth, the Frostfell, or the [[Land Under Eternal Ice]]—to distinguish them from the palace itself—and this region was fully under Auril's control. ==Geography== The realm of Winter's Hall was a frigid tundra fraught with violent winter storms,{{Cite book/Planes of Chaos/The Book of Chaos|93-94}} with winds rarely slower than 30 miles per hour. Visibility was only a few feet, because of the extreme blizzard conditions. As one traveled deeper into the realm, it grew colder and colder until the land was covered in a vast sheet of ice. It was said that there was no colder place in the multiverse, and anyone not taking shelter would take extreme damage from the bitter cold. Auril's palace itself was formed from ''[[wind wall]]s''{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|63}} and ice. It appeared like an inverted iceberg, hovering over the ground and surrounded in thick fog and freezing rain. Almost a mile in both diameter and height, it was the size of a small city. Huge crystalline extensions jutted out from the core of the fortress palace and were colored royal blue to sea green. The bottom surface of the floating palace included a giant window of shaped wind to view the ground below. Also located here was a dock for flying vessels, such as [[astraljammer]]s and [[airship]]s. The interior of the palace was a labyrinth of passageways. The Araamroth, or Promenade, was one of these, and it cut through the whole height of Winter's Hall, a latticework of pathways of crystal and support columns. The Promenade was lit by [[will-o'-wisp]] and other glowing creatures entrapped in ice globes. At the top of the Promenade was a dome of pure elemental ice. Auril could calm the winter storms surrounding the palace if she wanted the polar lights to be visible through the dome. At the base of the Promenade was a twin oscillating structure of chaos called the Abattoir, where bloody sacrifices were once performed in an attempt to trap [[Toril]] forever in darkness and ice. Deep within Winter's Hall was the Lyceum of Frozen Shadow, or Amon Thyryr, Aurils's throne room. Auril's throne itself was carved from frozen blue fire. The throne room was carved from the beating heart of the [[primordial]] [[Durbaagal]]. ==Inhabitants== [[Petitioner]]s of Auril took on the forms of cold elemental spirits, which were immune to [[cold]] and [[electricity]] and resistant to [[fire]] and [[sonic]] damage. These beings could inflict cold on anyone they touched. Nearly 20,000 such damned spirits resided within the palace walls alone. Other creatures of ice, such as cold element creatures and [[ice para-elemental]]s, also dwelt throughout the realm, as did [[frost giant]]s and an assortment of [[Wolf|wolves]], including [[Winter wolf|winter wolves]], normal wolves, [[worg]]s, and even [[Werewolf|werewolves]]. All canine monsters that entered the hall became ''charmed'' to obey its frost giant inhabitants and became servants of the frost giantess [[Ingrid the Serpent-Tongue]]. The pack of canines was led by [[White Fang]], an albino [[yeth hound]]. The [[Norse pantheon|Norse]] god [[Loki]] was said to sometimes make Winter's Hall his abode, as a place to hide away whenever he fell out of grace with the other [[Norse pantheon|Aesir]].{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|147}} While there, he often held feasts for the frost giants in his wooden hall of rough timber. Whenever he was away a [[cloud giant]] jarl by the name of [[Starkad the Gnawer]] would claim to be his proxy. Though many considered Ingrid to be the real power in the hall, as she led most of the Hall's hunts.{{Cite book/Planes of Chaos/The Book of Chaos|94-95}} ==Rumors & Legends== Winter's Hall was rumored to be the true source of the [[Styx]]. According to the legend, a mix of melting snow, divine [[poison]] and the blood of a tortured [[deity]] flowed into Pandemonium and became infused with the plane's [[evil]].{{Cite dragon/358/Savage Tidings: The River Styx|65}} ==Appendix== ===Appearances=== :;Card Games ::''[[Blood Wars]]'' ===References=== {{Refs}} ===Connections=== {{Pandemonium}} [[Category:Locations in Pandemonium]] [[Category:Locations in the Outer Planes]] [[Category:Locations in the Great Wheel planes]] [[Category:Locations in the Fiendish Planes]] [[Category:Locations in the World Tree planes]] [[Category:Locations on the River Styx]] [[Category:Locations in the Lower Planes]] [[Category:Locations on Yggdrasil]]

== History ==
Originally members of the [[w:c:dragonlance:Order of the Black Robes|Wizards of the Black Robes]], an order of evil mages from [[Krynn]], these women became frustrated by their male peers who felt superior due to their gender, and broke off to form their own group. They found by simply changing their attire, they could befuddle the simple-minded men they confronted.
They eventually moved to the planes where they became totally devoted to the [[Lady of Pain]], a trait which probably led to their eventual dissolution.

==Cosmography== In the [[Great Wheel cosmology]], Wonderhome was located in the [[Outlands]], though its exact placement within that [[plane]] was uncertain.<ref name="F&A-p62">{{Cite book/Faiths & Avatars|62}}</ref><ref name="OHG-p181">{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|181}}</ref><ref group="note" name="location">Wonderhome was never depicted on any maps of the Outlands, so its location in relation to all the other divine realms there is unknown.</ref> In the [[World Tree cosmology]], it was located in the [[celestial plane]] known as the [[House of Knowledge]], a plane that Gond shared with the Faerûnian deity of invention [[Oghma]].<ref name="PGtF-p158">{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|158}}</ref> And in the [[World Axis cosmology]], Wonderhome was also located within the House of Knowledge, but there the latter was considered to be an [[astral dominion]] belonging to Oghma.<ref name="FRCG-p64">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|64}}</ref>
A ''[[portal]]'' between this realm and the [[Mithral Forge]], divine realm of the [[gnome|gnomish]] craftsmen deity [[Flandal Steelskin]], was maintained by Gond.<ref name="PGtF-p158" />
==Description== Wonderhome was said to be a great workshop full of all manner of inventions. Some were recognizable to [[Faerûn]]ians, though many more were not as they had yet to be discovered.<ref name="PGtF-p158" />

{{Plane | image = Worldaxismodel.jpg | caption = ''A conceptual model of the World Axis cosmology'' | name = World Axis cosmology | type = [[Cosmology]] | natives = | alignment trait = | gravity trait = | time trait = | shape & size = | morphic = | faith trait = | elemental & energy traits = | magical trait = }} The '''World Axis''' was a cosmological model created after the dramatic changes to the nature of the multiverse caused by the [[Spellplague]] of [[1385 DR]],<ref name="FRCG-p50">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|50}}</ref> and quickly became the most widely accepted model during the late years of the 14{{Th}} century [[DR]] and for most of the 15{{Th}} century.<ref name="FRCG-p62"/>
This structure, which resembled a sphere split into two axes—hence the name—resulted from the Spellplague and its effects upon the local multiverse, which included the untethering of the [[astral dominion]]s<ref name="FRCG-p62">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|62}}</ref> and the creation (or possible return<ref name="FRCG-Elemental Chaos"/>) of the [[Elemental Chaos]]. As a result of the changes wrought by the disaster, the formerly prominent [[World Tree]] model was abandoned in favor of the World Axis, which most scholars believed more accurately reflected the current structure of the multiverse.<ref name="FRCG-Introduction">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|4–5}}</ref><ref name="FRCG-Cosmology">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|60}}</ref>
After the [[Second Sundering]] of the late years of the 15{{Th}} century, some sages began to use again the older World Tree and [[Great Wheel cosmology|Great Wheel]] models, however the World Axis remained as one of the most popular cosmological models used by scholars who studied the nature of the multiverse.<ref name="DMG5e">{{Cite book/Dungeon Master's Guide 5th edition|43-43}}</ref><ref name="Jeremy">{{cite web|author=[[Jeremy Crawford]]|title=Jeremy's Twitter|url=https://twitter.com/JeremyECrawford/status/558443947815489536|accessdate=2018-01-25}}</ref>
==Basic Structure== The World Axis was composed primarily of the [[Fundamental plane|fundamental]] and [[parallel plane]]s. "Above" and "below," the fundamental planes encircled the rest of the cosmology, forming hemispheres in the conceptual model, though since both the [[Astral Sea]] and the Elemental Chaos were infinite in size, this was mostly metaphorical. To the "left" and the "right" of the [[Prime Material Plane]], which laid at the center of this cosmology, sit the parallel planes, which floated in sync with the Prime. Together these planes formed the World Axis, other planes lying outside of the model and having an indistinct cosmological placement.<ref name="MotP4e-p12">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|12}}</ref>
The World Axis was similar in many ways to the World Tree that came before it. Like the World Tree, the World Axis model placed the astral dominions "above" the Prime while placing the [[elemental plane|elemental]] and [[energy plane]]s, the precursors of the Elemental Chaos, "below." Likewise, the [[Plane of Shadow]], the [[Shadowfell]]'s precedent, existed in close sync with the Prime.<ref name="MotP4e-p12"/>
However, differences existed. While the astral dominions, elemental planes, and energy planes were all formerly bound together in a tree-like structure, the Spellplague destroyed these bonds,<ref name="FRCG-p50"/> causing the astral dominions to float freely through the Astral Sea.<ref name="FRCG-p64">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|64}}</ref> Similarly, the Spellplague caused the elemental and energy planes to fall into one another and to fuse with an elemental plane from [[Abeir]], causing them to become one indistinct, ever-changing plane.<ref name="FRCG-Elemental Chaos"/> The Shadowfell was also created out of the Plane of Shadow, incorporating into it some of the [[Negative Energy Plane]]'s energy,<ref name="FRCG-p69">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|69}}</ref> and the [[Feywild]], nearly forgotten for millennia, came back into sync with the Prime, regaining its place as a parallel plane.<ref name="FRCG-p68">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|68}}</ref>
==Prime Material Plane== {{main|Prime Material Plane}}
Also called the natural world, mortal world, or simply the Prime, this plane laid at the center of the World Axis. While changed, the Prime continued to exist in spite of the changes wrought by the Spellplague, stable and at the center of the vast axes that binded the planes together. The Prime was where [[Toril]] and its inhabitants were located and remained the primary focus of the [[deity|god]]s. The Prime had no single dominant force, unlike most planes, and was connected to the other planes through the Shadowfell and, to a lesser extent, the Astral Sea and Elemental Chaos.<ref name="MotP4e-p12"/>
==Fundamental Planes== {{main|Fundamental plane}}
Surrounding the Prime and the parallel planes were the two fundamental planes: the Astral Sea and the Elemental Chaos.<ref name="MotP4e-p12">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|12}}</ref> The fundamental planes, according to common theory, were the basis from which all the other planes, including the Prime and its echoes, were formed.<ref name="MotP4e-p8">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|8}}</ref> Whether or not this was true is unsure{{Speculation}} and until the Spellplague, the Elemental Chaos was not believed to have existed, or at least not since the splitting of [[Abeir-Toril]] into two worlds.<ref name="FRCG-Elemental Chaos"/>
The fundamental planes were also the homes of the [[astral dominion]]s and elemental realms, smaller planes within the Astral Sea and Elemental Chaos. Only a few of these were known to the inhabitants of Toril, however, and it is believed that if one traveled far enough through the infinite spaces of the fundamental planes it might be possible to locate the dominions and realms of entirely different pantheons worshiped by beings from other material planes, though such a journey would be unimaginably lengthy.<ref name="MotP4e-p8">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|8}}</ref>
The two fundamental planes are as follows:
;[[Astral Sea|The Astral Sea]] :The Astral Sea was a great silvery void that contained the homes of the [[Deity|gods]] and which was considered the realm of pure thought and creativity, where thoughts and feelings became reality, if only for a moment. It was through this power that gods shaped the cosmos according to their will and the astral dominions were forged.<ref name="MotP4e-p84">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|84}}</ref> ;[[Elemental Chaos|The Elemental Chaos]] :Nonexistent before the Spellplague, or at least not since the sundering of Abeir-Toril,<ref name="FRCG-Elemental Chaos">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|66–67}}</ref> the Elemental Chaos was a vast and infinite sea of tempestuous matter and energy in which the cycle of creation and destruction continued without end. It was from the essence of the chaos that the world was first formed, tempered though it was by the divine essences of the Astral Sea.<ref name="MotP4e-p84">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|84}}</ref>
===Astral Dominions=== {{main|Astral dominion}}
Within the Astral Sea laid the astral dominions, planes separated and unique from the surrounding fundamental plane but which owed their existence to it. Formed from the will of the Astral Sea's inhabitants<ref name="MotP4e-p12">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|12}}</ref> the astral dominions were once linked into an intricate network within the World Tree. As a result of the Spellplague, the formerly bound planes drifted freely in the Astral Sea.<ref name="FRCG-p62">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|62}}</ref>
There were many dominions within the Astral Sea, the known ones being as follows:
;[[Arvandor]] :Arvandor was the home of the [[Seldarine|elven pantheon]], the [[Lords of the Golden Hills|gnomish pantheon]], and several [[archfey]]. [[Corellon]] ruled over this good plane with his wife, the goddess [[Angharradh]], while [[Garl Glittergold]] held his own, somewhat independent court.<ref name="FRCG-p62">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|62}}</ref> ;[[Banehold]] :Banehold was the home of the Black Lord [[Bane]], who ruled from his keep the Black Bastion, as well as the gods who owed their fealty to him. The evil plane was surrounded by outlying wastelands that served as a warning to these subjugated deities.<ref name="FRCG-p62">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|62}}</ref> ;[[Celestia]] :Celestia was an enormous mountain that contained three smaller peaks. The True Court was a city near the top of the mountain, from which [[Torm]] ruled the [[lawful good]] plane alongside [[Ilmater]] and [[Bahamut]].<ref name="FRCG-p62">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|62}}</ref> ;[[Cynosure]] :Cynosure was a neutral meeting place of the gods and was usually closed and uninhabited. Cynosure was merely a stately meeting chamber full of high pillars and decorated with portraits of gods and goddesses both living and dead.<ref name="FRCG-p62-63">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|62–63}}</ref> ;[[Deep Wilds|The Deep Wilds]] :The [[Deep Wilds]] was the home of [[Silvanus]] and his divine servants. The Deep Wilds were a vast expanse of untamed and wild wilderness, with no strong ties to any alignment but firm connections to several elemental realms.<ref name="FRCG-p63">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|63}}</ref> ;[[Demonweb Pits|The Demonweb Pits]] :The Demonweb Pits was [[Lolth]]’s domain and a former layer of [[Abyss|the Abyss]]. This strongly chaotic evil plane was an immense and dark dominion of woven planar matter, at the center of which sit Lolth’s arachnid-shaped iron fortress.<ref name="FRCG-p63">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|63}}</ref> ;[[Dismal Caverns|The Dismal Caverns]] :The Dismal Caverns were a huge subterranean maze of natural caverns, ruled over by the solitary god [[Ghaunadaur]]. Other powerful entities, many [[aberration]]s touched by the [[Far Realm]], also lived there, dwelling in the vast darkness that filled the plane.<ref name="FRCG-p63">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|63}}</ref> ;[[Dwarfhome]] :Dwarfhome was the home of the [[Morndinsamman|dwarven deities]] and their worshipers, who dwelt underneath massive mountainous crags teeming with life. At the heart of Dwarfhome was the great hall called Erackinor, the residence of [[Moradin]] and his wife [[Berronar]].<ref name="FRCG-p63">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|63}}</ref> ;[[Eternal Sun]] :Eternal Sun was the dominion of [[Amaunator]], Keeper of the Golden Sun, who shared the realm with [[Waukeen]] and his [[exarch]], [[Siamorphe]]. Amaunator made his home in the Palace of the Four Suns, the central citadel of a golden city which was located amid shining, thriving lands and seas.<ref name="FRCG-p63">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|63}}</ref> ;[[Fugue Plane|The Fugue Plane]] :The Fugue Plane was a flat and featureless plane with a ground of silvery mist. It was here that the god [[Kelemvor]] judged the dead, who arrived through the [[Shadowfell]], either releasing them to the blessings of their god or sentencing them to eternal punishment.<ref name="FRCG-p63">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|63}}</ref> ;[[Gates of the Moon]] :Gates of the Moon consisted of rocky islands that floated on and above a silvery sea, over which the moon waxed and waned constantly. It was here that the [[chaotic good]] [[greater deity|greater goddess]]es [[Selûne]] and [[Sune]] both made their home, along with the goddess [[Tymora]].<ref name="FRCG-p63">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|63}}</ref> ;[[Green Fields]] :Green Fields was a place of rest, of lush valleys and hills ruled over by the Earthmother [[Chauntea]]. The [[halfling pantheon]] also resided here, moving from place to place like their mortal worshipers.<ref name="FRCG-p64" /> ;[[House of Knowledge]] :The House of Knowledge consisted of an ancient and tamed wood of giant oak trees and clear and fresh lakes and springs. A series of buildings throughout the dominion called the Library of All Knowledge was said to contain all the secrets of the multiverse.<ref name="FRCG-p64" /> ;[[Nine Hells|The Nine Hells]] :The Nine Hells, or Baator as its denizens called it, was the home of [[devil]]s and is ruled by [[Asmodeus]],<ref name="FRCG-p62-65">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|62–65}}</ref> a former god-turned-[[Archdevils|archdevil]]-turned-god-again<ref name="FRCG-Asmodeus">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|73}}</ref> who resided in Malsheem, the Citadel of Hell. Eight other archdevils ruled eight other layers of the [[lawful evil]] dominion as vassals of Asmodeus.<ref name="FRCG-p64" /> ;[[Nishrek]] :Nishrek was home to the [[orc pantheon]], ruled over by the savage god [[Gruumsh]]. This [[chaotic evil]] plane resembled a natural setting ravaged by eternal war, filled with of scorching deserts, jagged badlands, and dense and tangled forests, with black seas and rivers.<ref name="FRCG-p64" /> ;[[Supreme Throne|The Supreme Throne]] :The Supreme Throne was [[Cyric]]’s dominion but it was also a prison for the Prince of Lies, whose murder of [[Mystra]] had resulted in his internment for several centuries to come. The dominion was sealed off by the other gods, and none could enter nor could any leave.<ref name="FRCG-p64-65">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|64–65}}</ref> ;[[Towers of Night]] :Towers of Night was the largest of the astral dominions, a vast and dark wasteland composed of mountainous regions, deserts of black sand, and malevolent seas, rivers, forests, and bogs. Ruling over this plane was the greater goddess [[Shar]], who shared the [[neutral evil]] dominion with her servants [[Sseth]], [[Talona]], and [[Zehir]].<ref name="FRCG-p65">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|65}}</ref> ;[[Tu'Narath]] :Unlike the divine dominions where the gods reside Tu'Narath was a realm shaped by mortal minds, specifically those of the [[githyanki]]. Within the great metropolis carved from the corpse of a forgotten god the githyanki were ruled over by their [[lich]]-queen [[Vlaakith]], who constantly plotted for the conquest of the other planes and who hold ''de facto'' control of the other nominally independent githyanki settlements.<ref name="MotP4e-p111">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|111}}</ref> ;[[Warrior's Rest]] :Warrior’s Rest was the dominion of [[Tempus]], god of war and his nature shaped the plane into a landscape nearly as chaotic and unpredictable as the Elemental Chaos, constantly changing. The souls of warriors who worshiped Tempus or other human war deities lived here, always waging wars dying again and again in endless battle only to rise again while the victorious celebrated in the many halls that dot the landscape.<ref name="FRCG-p65">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|65}}</ref>
===Elemental Realms=== {{main|Elemental realm}} When the elemental and energy planes collided to form, or possibly reform, the Elemental Chaos most of them were lost, along with the other planes that fell into the mix, such as [[Limbo]] or [[Jotunheim]]. However, within the Chaos those beings strong enough and powerful enough to shape the materials around them were able to create new planes or preserve parts of old ones, either of which became known as elemental realms. Here numerous elemental creatures resided, alongside the mighty [[primordial]]s who first created the planes alongside the gods.<ref name="MotP4e-p13">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|13}}</ref>
The known elemental realms are listed below:
;[[Abyss|The Abyss]] :The Abyss was the home of [[demon]]s and was ruled over by none, though several of the powerful [[demon lord]]s each claimed control. A multi-layered pit, the Abyss laid at the very "bottom" of the Elemental Chaos, waiting to draw in and ensnare any who came too close.<ref name="FRCG-p66">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|66}}</ref> ;[[City of Brass|The City of Brass]] :The City of Brass was the home of the [[efreeti]], fire [[genie]]s who long ago forged this city, which was believed the oldest in all the planes. Though efreeti were known for their wars against other elementals, the City of Brass was best known as the center of interplanar trade.<ref name="MotP4e-p73">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|73}}</ref> ;[[Cresting Spires]] :Dominated by the primordial [[Istishia]], the Cresting Spires were a plane dominated by water.<ref name="FRCG-p66">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|66}}</ref> ;[[Fimbulwinter]] :Forged by the [[titan]] [[Thrym]], this plane was covered in ice.<ref name="FRCG-p67">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|67}}</ref> ;[[Hidden Realm]] :The most powerful of the titans, [[Annam]], ruled this mysterious realm.<ref name="FRCG-p67">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|67}}</ref> ;[[Muspelheim]] :Ruled over by the titan [[Surtr]], Muspelheim was dominated by a volcanic landscape.<ref name="FRCG-p67">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|67}}</ref> ;[[Root Hold]] :Dominated by [[Grumbar]], the primordial lord of the [[Earth domain|earth element]], Root Hold was a series of vast subterranean halls with strong connections to the Dismal Caverns and Dwarfhome.<ref name="FRCG-p66">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|66}}</ref> ;[[Sky Home]] :A realm ruled over by the primordial [[Akadi]] and dominated by rolling clouds and dark storms. Sky Home had links to the plane of [[Arvandor]].<ref name="FRCG-p66">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|66}}</ref> ;[[Steading]] :This realm resembled a landscape of rolling hills and was dominated by the titan [[Grolantor]].<ref name="FRCG-p67">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|67}}</ref> ;[[Thraotor]] :A plane of [[Storm domain|storms]] this plane was ruled over by the titan [[Memnor]].<ref name="FRCG-p67">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|67}}</ref> ;[[Undying Pyre|The Undying Pyre]] :The Undying Pyre was a fiery plane of thick smoke and mighty flames, ruled over by the strongest of the primordial lords, [[Kossuth]].<ref name="FRCG-p66">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|66}}</ref> ;[[Zerthadlun]] :Zerthadlun was a realm shaped by the minds and will of the [[githzerai]], mortals who had taken residence in the Elemental Chaos in order to study the entropy that filled it. Through constant diligence and monastic ritual the githzerai maintained their realm, in spite of the chaos that threatened to engulf it.<ref name="MotP4e-p77">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|77}}</ref>
==Parallel Planes== {{main|Parallel plane}}
Parallel planes were strange reflections of the Prime, formed by the will of the primordials in the age of creation who gathered what they considered to be imperfections of the Prime and created new planes from them. Parallel planes were the closest of the planes to the Prime and resembled it geographically, though they were very distinct in their own manner.<ref name="MotP4e-p8">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|8}}</ref>
The parallel planes were:
;[[Feywild|The Feywild]] :A vibrant twin of the Prime, the Feywild was the home of the [[fey]] and was filled with vitality and powerful [[arcane magic]].<ref name="MotP4e-p32">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|32}}</ref> ;[[Shadowfell|The Shadowfell]] :A dark and twisted echo of the Prime formed by [[Shar]] from the [[Plane of Shadow]] and part of the [[Negative Energy Plane]], the Shadowfell was the home of shadow creatures as well as much of the [[undead]] that filled the planes.<ref name="FRCG-p69">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|69}}</ref>
==Transitive Planes==
These planes had little in common, except for their most common use: getting from one plane to another. A great number of spells that allowed travel from one plane to another briefly send travelers through one of the transitive planes before they reached their destination. Since the Spellplague the use of the term transitive plane had fallen out of disfavor, though the name's meaning still applied.
;[[Astral Sea]] :The Astral Sea served as a transitive plane between the astral dominions, much as it did prior to the Spellplague, though now the dominions drifted freely.<ref name="FRCG-p62">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|62}}</ref> ;[[Elemental Chaos]] : Similarly, the Elemental Chaos allowed travel between the elemental realms.<ref name="FRCG-p66">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|66}}</ref> ;[[Shadowfell]] :The Shadowfell, in addition to serving as a strange and dark echo of the Prime also was a stop for many planar travelers. Most commonly this purpose was served for the recently dead, who passed through the Shadowfell on their way to judgment in the Fugue Plane.<ref name="FRCG-p69">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|69}}</ref>
